When the six-wheeled Tyrrell P34 made its debut
at the first European Grand Prix in Spain in 1976, it
caused a sensation. Derek Gardner’s idea of fitting
four small, steerable front wheels to a Formula 1
car was nothing short of a revolution. Whilst team-
mate Jody Scheckter was still driving the old Tyrrell
007, Patrick Depailler sensationally qualified the
new car in third place on the grid at its debut in
Jarama.
From Zolder onwards, two P34s lined up on the
starting grid, but the new design also caused the
drivers some trouble: they could not see the small
front wheels when turning in. Tyrrell therefore
fitted small windows into the cockpit below the
mirrors. This problem was solved.
The retrofitted revolutio

However, the revolutionary six-wheel Tyrrell’s aero-
dynamic advantages came at the cost of drawbacks
such as the added weight of the complex front-axle
design and difficulties in developing specialised
tyres with Goodyear. Although Jody Scheckter won
in Sweden, the car remained problematic. When
cooling problems arose, Derek Gardner had to fit
an additional radiator at the front of Scheckter’s
car at Zandvoort.
The brand-new design had to be retrofitted with
old-fashioned solutions, resulting in a rather odd
appearance. Still, Jody Scheckter finished fifth at
the Dutch GP and at the end of the year the South
African came third in the 1976 World Champion-
ship.

Enzo’s sweet revenge
Ford’s one-two-three finish at the 1966 Le Mans
24 Hours had deeply wounded Enzo Ferrari’s
Italian pride. For many years, the Italians had
dominated the endurance classic, only having to
bow to the superiority of the armada of Ford Mk Ils
fielded in 1966. The fact that all three of the new
beautiful Ferrari 330 P3s had retired was regarded
as a disaster in Maranello.
Enzo Ferrari therefore demanded revenge for this
humiliation as early as the first World Champion-
ship round of the 1967 season. In early February
1967, the rivals clashed once more at the Daytona
24 Hours: six 7-litre V8 Ford Mk Ils against three
works Ferraris with their 4-litre V12 engines.
Rarely has there been a more impressive cam-
paign of revenge in motorsport, as Ferrari inflicted
a crushing defeat on the giant Ford on its home
ground. Trailing by 73 laps, the best-placed Ford
Mk II finished a distant seventh.
The Ferrari 330 P3/4 Spyder, driven by Lorenzo
Bandini and Chris Amon, won the race, three laps
ahead of the #24, the 330 P4 with Mike Parkes and
Ludovico Scarfiotti at the wheel. Finishing third,
the 412P entered by American N.A.R.T. team, with
Pedro Rodriguez and Jean Guichet completed the
Italian one-two-three victory. The humiliation of Le
Mans 1966 had not been forgotten, but Enzo Fer-
rari had taken a fitting revenge.
